benchmarks.label: Open Philanthropy GHW funding bar (~$50 per DALY, 2023)
benchmarks.source_title: Our planned allocation to GiveWell's recommendations for the next few years
benchmarks.publisher: Open Philanthropy (Alexander Berger and Emily Oehlsen), cross-posted on the Effective Altruism Forum
benchmarks.quote: That means we need to be averting a DALY for ~$50 (because we value DALYs at $100K)
benchmarks.notes: Approximate ('~$50') funding bar for Open Philanthropy's Global Health & Wellbeing grantmaking after it raised its bar to 'slightly over 2000x' in 2023. Funder's internal threshold, not a measured intervention cost. The canonical openphilanthropy.org URL now redirects to coefficientgiving.org (Open Philanthropy rebranded as Coefficient Giving), which returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher, so the official EA Forum cross-post by the same authors was used. The bar may have changed since 2023; not checked against newer posts.

benchmarks.label: Open Philanthropy 1,000x bar (~$100 per DALY, 2021)
benchmarks.source_title: Technical Updates to Our Global Health and Wellbeing Cause Prioritization Framework
benchmarks.publisher: Open Philanthropy (Alexander Berger), cross-posted on the Effective Altruism Forum
benchmarks.quote: an intervention could meet 1000x by averting 1 DALY for every $100 in spending
benchmarks.notes: From a footnote illustrating the earlier 'roughly 1,000x' bar given a DALY valued at $100,000. Superseded by the 2023 ~$50/DALY bar (the primary benchmark); kept as a historical reference point. Illustrative threshold, not an intervention estimate.

benchmarks.label: GiveDirectly-style cash transfers, local multiplier 2.5 (Egger et al. 2022)
benchmarks.source_title: General Equilibrium Effects of Cash Transfers: Experimental Evidence From Kenya
benchmarks.publisher: Econometrica (Econometric Society), Vol. 90, No. 6, pp. 2603-2643; Egger, Haushofer, Miguel, Niehaus, Walker
benchmarks.quote: We estimate a local transfer multiplier of 2.5.
benchmarks.notes: RCT of ~USD 1,000 one-time GiveDirectly transfers to over 10,500 households in 653 villages in rural Kenya. The multiplier is the increase in local economic activity (recipients and non-recipients) per $1 transferred, not per $1 donated: GiveDirectly's overhead is not included, so per donated dollar the figure would be somewhat lower. It measures local GDP/expenditure, not only recipient income. Earlier working-paper versions reported 2.4-2.8 ('fiscal multiplier'); the published 2.5 is used here.

benchmarks.label: GiveDirectly summary: $2.60 local spending/income per $1 delivered (2019)
benchmarks.source_title: New research results: How do cash transfers impact the people who don't receive them?
benchmarks.quote: $1 of cash delivered generated $2.60 in additional spending or income for the local economy.
benchmarks.notes: Charity's own summary of the 2019 working-paper version of Egger et al. Per $1 delivered (not donated). The same page also quotes the abstract's 'local fiscal multiplier of 2.5'; the page notes an updated version was published in November 2022. Use the Econometrica figure (primary) for comparisons.

charities.name: Against Malaria Foundation
charities.program: Distribution of long-lasting insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent malaria
charities.quote: these donations would avert a DALY for approximately $78 in expectation
charities.notes: OUTDATED: the page is dated 20 Jun 2016 and says it is no longer updated. Derived from a then-current GiveWell estimate of $3,461 per under-5 death averted. The same page also walks through a simpler calculation ($3,461 / 36.5 discounted life-years, 3% discount rate) giving $95, so the $78 figure depends on the page's own modelling choices. GiveWell's current Top Charities page (last updated Sept 2025) gives 'an estimated average cost-effectiveness of $5,500 per life saved' for AMF (2022-2024 funding), which suggests the cost per DALY today is higher than $78. GiveWell itself does not publish a cost per DALY. Treat as an estimate in nominal USD of the time.

charities.name: Malaria Consortium (Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention)
charities.program: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) for young children; Nampula province, Mozambique, 2023 campaign
charities.source_title: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention in northern Mozambique: a cost-effectiveness analysis (Malaria Journal 24; DOI 10.1186/s12936-025-05401-x)
charities.publisher: Malaria Journal (BMC/Springer Nature); Canana N et al., first author affiliated with Malaria Consortium
charities.quote: the estimated cost was $93.50 per malaria case averted, $3286.59 per malaria death averted, and $130.16 per DALY averted.
charities.notes: Peer-reviewed study by the charity's own staff of one country/one year (Mozambique 2023); not a whole-organization average. DALYs estimated using Global Burden of Disease 2019 data. Cost year, perspective and discount rate were not verified (the PMC, Springer and DOAJ pages blocked the fetcher; the abstract was read via the Europe PMC API, the URL given). Other SMC studies cited in search results range roughly $19-$183 per DALY by country. GiveWell's Top Charities page (Sept 2025) gives 'an estimated average cost-effectiveness of $4,000 per life saved' for Malaria Consortium SMC.

charities.name: Helen Keller Intl (Vitamin A Supplementation)
charities.program: Vitamin A supplementation campaigns for children aged 6-59 months
charities.quote: an estimated average cost-effectiveness of $3,500 per life saved
charities.notes: MISSING: no charity-specific cost per DALY found. GiveWell (above, 2022-2024 funding) gives cost per life saved only; per instructions this was not converted to DALYs. Founders Pledge's HKI page (updated 2021-11-12) repeats GiveWell's '$3,000-$5,000 donated' per life, with no DALY figure. Searched GiveWell, Founders Pledge and general web for 'per DALY'.

charities.name: New Incentives
charities.program: Conditional cash incentives for routine childhood vaccination in northern Nigeria
charities.quote: an estimated average cost-effectiveness of $4,500 per life saved
charities.notes: MISSING: no cost per DALY found. GiveWell reports cost per life saved (above, 2022-2024 funding) and multiples of cash; not converted to DALYs per instructions.

charities.name: Evidence Action - Deworm the World Initiative
charities.program: School-based mass deworming for soil-transmitted helminths and schistosomiasis
charities.source_title: Evidence Action's Deworm the World Initiative
charities.quote: deworming medication is sufficiently cheap (between $0.34 and $1.52 per treatment)
charities.notes: MISSING: no current charity-specific cost per DALY found; the source gives cost per treatment only. GiveWell values deworming mainly through long-run income effects, not DALYs. Historical deworming cost-per-DALY figures (DCP2 ~$3.41, corrected ~$326) were contested after errors were found, so they are not used.

charities.name: GiveDirectly
charities.program: Unconditional cash transfers (~USD 1,000) to poor households, rural Kenya (GE study)
charities.source_title: New research results: How do cash transfers impact the people who don't receive them?
charities.quote: We estimate a local fiscal multiplier of 2.5.
charities.notes: Same study as the poverty primary benchmark (Egger et al.; published Econometrica Nov 2022 with 'local transfer multiplier of 2.5'). Per $1 transferred, not per $1 donated (overhead not included). Measures total local economic activity, not only recipient income. The same page also states '$2.60 in additional spending or income' per $1 delivered.

charities.name: Village Enterprise
charities.program: Microenterprise graduation program (business groups, cash grants, training), Kenya and Uganda; Development Impact Bond RCT
charities.source_title: Frequently Asked Questions about the Village Enterprise Development Impact Bond
charities.quote: Our three-year benefit-cost ratio (BCR) of 140% represents significant progress toward this goal.
charities.notes: Self-reported by the charity, based on the third-party (IDinsight) DIB RCT. 140% BCR recorded as $1.40 of benefit per $1 of program cost. The page does not define the calculation; benefits likely include household consumption/spending and net wealth (assets), not only income, measured over three years. Cost is program implementation cost, not necessarily total donated dollars. The same page says projected lifetime benefit is 'over five times the cost to implement the program' (a projection, not used). Stored as $100 cost -> $140 benefit (140%); the app's calculator divides.

charities.name: Bandhan (Targeting the Hard-Core Poor graduation program, West Bengal)
charities.program: 18-month ultra-poor graduation program (asset transfer, consumption support, training, coaching), West Bengal, India
charities.source_title: Graduating the Ultra Poor in India
charities.publisher: Innovations for Poverty Action (study page for Banerjee et al. 2015, Science)
charities.quote: total implementation and program costs to be US$330 per household (2014 PPP US$ 1,455) … estimated benefits from consumption and asset growth amount to 2014 PPP US$6,298 per household, representing an overall 433 percent return.
charities.notes: Per household, in 2014 PPP USD; cost from the same page: 'total implementation and program costs to be US$330 per household (2014 PPP US$ 1,455)'. Both inputs are PPP-adjusted, so the ratio (about 4.33) is in PPP terms; at market exchange rates the cost was $330. Benefits are consumption plus asset growth (projected long-run), not only income. Per program cost, not per dollar donated. India site of the six-country Science 2015 RCT; the benefit-cost assumptions (duration, discount rate) were not checked in the paper itself. Quote joins two verbatim passages from the same page (cost, then benefits).

charities.name: BRAC Ultra-Poor Graduation (Bangladesh)
charities.program: Ultra-poor graduation program: livestock/asset transfer, stipend, training and coaching, Bangladesh
charities.source_title: Graduation: What's next for ultra-poor programmes?
charities.publisher: International Growth Centre (Emilie Yam, Upaasna Kaul, Amanda Jinhage)
charities.quote: In this scenario, each dollar spent generates 5.7 dollars of benefits.
charities.notes: MISSING: no single defensible figure. This secondary blog reports Oriana Bandiera's two scenarios: $5.7 per $1 if benefits last forever, but 'only 80 cents' per $1 if benefits evaporate after four years. A BRAC Institute (BIGD) study page on the credit-plus-grant variant reports 'benefits on average 4.59 times higher than its costs' but its Findings section gives 7.11 for the same program, which is inconsistent. BRAC's own Graduation impact brief (fetched as PDF) gives no benefit-cost ratio. Left missing rather than choose between conflicting or scenario-dependent values.

charities.name: One Acre Fund
charities.program: Smallholder farmer support: inputs on credit, training and market access in East Africa
charities.quote: Social Return on Investment: $5.7 new farm profits created for every $1 of donor investment.
charities.notes: Self-reported, not independently verified; method not explained on the page. Denominator is donor funding only (farmer loan repayments cover much of the program cost), so this is per dollar donated, which flatters it compared with per-total-cost figures. Outcome is new farm profits, not total household income. No date is given for the figure (page footer (c) 2026; nearby metrics refer to 2025). Search results showed earlier self-reported values of $3.20 (2022) and $4.43 (2024), so the figure changes from year to year.
